newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Sales talk swirls round Olivetti.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sales talk swirls round Olivetti.

text.p: Sales talk swirled around struggling Italian information technology group Olivetti on Friday but weary investors, fearing another cash call sooner rather than later, steadily sold the stock.

One week after chief executive Roberto Colaninno said Olivetti thought it had found a buyer for its personal computer business, a report in Milan daily MF fuelled speculation that Taiwanese computer giant Acer could be about to bid.
But Acer's Italian country manager told Reuters that the group, which sometimes supplies to Olivetti, was not interested.
"There have been no discussions specific to buying the PC business," he said.
"They are our friends in the industry and we talk to them. We are not talking about the PC business," he added.
Dealers said the swell of rumour after rumour in recent days had left jaded international investors fed up and no longer knowing what to believe, prompting a wave of selling.
"There's a lot of speculation," said one trader. "It's very difficult to tell what is real business and what is just trading back and forth."
Olivetti shares plunged nearly seven percent to 445 lire (28 cents) before recovering ground in late trade to stand 3.75 percent lower at 459.5 lire, with 38.4 million shares changing hands.
"No-one wants it," said another analyst. "Technical analysts believe the stock could go as far down as 350 (lire)."

Dealers said the market were worried that Olivetti may soon ask its long-suffering shareholders to stump up yet more cash by the end of the 1996 -- just one year after it launched a massive rescue rights issue of 2.26 trillion lire ($1.47 billion).
Colaninno said last week that one group was attracted by the PC division and was studying a bid.

But he said that asset sales -- which Olivetti reckons will raise 800 billion lire this year and a further 400 billion next year -- would not bring the company back to break even and a capital increase could be needed at the end of 1997.
"People think he got it wrong and he meant the end of 1996," said one dealer.
Analysts believe Olivetti's PC business is worth nothing to sell but were seeking a disposal for a nominal sum to avoid the certain outcry that would follow shutting it down.
Olivetti workers meanwhile took to the streets in Rome for a national demonstration and staged an eight-hour strike in protest at the group's precarious future.

"We won't let our guard down and we won't lie down and accept the sale of bits of a company that belongs to the whole country to the first person who comes along," said Luigi Angeletti, secretary general of the UILM union.

Acer's denial of interest in the PC unit, which lost 200 billion lire last year and was 10 billion lire in the red in the first half of 1996, came hot on the heels of similar denials last week by Japanese groups NEC and Sony.

Further speculation had also flared on Thursday when Il Messaggero newspaper reported that Mediaset, the media group controlled by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, was mulling a takeover of Olivetti to boost its mobile phone hopes.
Analysts see Olivetti's controlling stake in the successful cellular phone venture Omnitel as its most attractive asset.
But Mediaset quashed the talk. "We have no interest at present in taking over Olivetti," managing director Ubaldo Livolsi said on Friday.
($ = 1535 Italian Lire)
